title: The Firmware Landscape: Betaflight, INAV, ArduPilot, PX4 & DJI
html:
Flight controllers run software, not magic

The flight controller (FC) is a small computer running an MCU like the STM32F405, F722, or the newer H743. The firmware on that chip reads the gyro/accelerometer (IMU), reads your receiver, runs a control loop hundreds or thousands of times per second, and outputs motor commands to the ESCs. Choosing firmware is choosing a philosophy: razor-sharp manual control, or GPS-assisted autonomy.

The five players

FirmwareBest forDifficulty
BetaflightFreestyle, racing, cinematic 5" quadsBeginner-friendly
INAVGPS multirotors, fixed-wing, long-range, return-to-homeModerate
ArduPilotAutonomous missions, mapping, heavy-lift, boats/roversAdvanced
PX4Research, commercial drones, professional autonomyAdvanced
DJI (closed)Camera drones, O3/O4 air units, ready-to-flyPlug-and-play

Betaflight

The default for FPV freestyle and racing. It prioritizes low latency and crisp stick response over autonomy. It is open source, has a huge community, and the Configurator GUI makes setup approachable. It supports GPS for rescue (return-to-home on signal loss) but is not a survey or waypoint platform.

INAV

A Betaflight fork that adds serious navigation: waypoint missions, GPS position hold, altitude hold, and robust return-to-home. INAV is the go-to for fixed-wing planes and GPS "cruiser" multirotors. The PID/feel is less razor-sharp than Betaflight, which is fine for autonomous flying.

ArduPilot & PX4

These are full autonomy stacks used in commercial, agricultural, and research drones. They run on Pixhawk-class hardware, integrate with ground-control software (Mission Planner, QGroundControl), and support planes, copters, rovers, and boats. Steep learning curve, but unmatched for autonomous missions.

DJI ecosystem

DJI uses closed firmware on products like the O3/O4 Air Unit and full camera drones. You configure through the DJI Fly/Goggles app, not a desktop tool. You trade tunability for reliability and image quality. Note: the FPV-side O3/O4 air unit can pair with a Betaflight FC for the flight side while DJI handles the video.

Rule of thumb.
If you fly with your hands and eyes (freestyle/racing), pick Betaflight. If the drone should fly itself or hold position, pick INAV (hobby) or ArduPilot/PX4 (professional).
Regulation note.
Autonomy features do not exempt you from Remote ID, registration, or airspace rules. Verify current FAA Part 107/recreational rules (or your national CAA) before any beyond-line-of-sight or automated flight.
▸Hands-On

Build a firmware decision matrix and pick yours.

  1. List your build's goal (freestyle, GPS plane, autonomous mapping, camera).
  2. Make a table: firmware vs. use case, hardware support (does your FC target exist?), and difficulty.
  3. Check your FC's product page for which firmware targets it ships with.
  4. Circle the single firmware you'll flash and write one sentence justifying it.

title: Flashing Betaflight & the Configurator Tour
html:
Get the tools

Install the Betaflight Configurator (the desktop app, or the Chrome/standalone build) and the Betaflight Blackbox Explorer. On Windows you also need the Zadig driver tool so the FC's DFU bootloader is recognized; on macOS/Linux drivers usually just work.

Enter bootloader (DFU)

To flash, the FC must be in DFU (Device Firmware Update) mode. Two ways:

  • Hold the BOOT button on the FC while plugging in USB.
  • Or connect normally, then in the Configurator's Firmware Flasher click the device dropdown and select DFU.

When in DFU, the port dropdown shows DFU instead of a COM/tty port.

Pick the right target

This is the #1 way people brick a board: flashing the wrong target. The target is the board name (e.g., SPEEDYBEEF405V4, STM32F405). Find your exact FC model in its documentation. In the Firmware Flasher, select the target, the latest stable release, and read the release notes.

Props OFF, always.
Never have propellers installed while connected to USB or testing motors. A firmware glitch or accidental arm can spin a prop into your fingers.

Flash settings

Firmware Flasher
Target: SPEEDYBEEF405V4 Version: 4.5.x (Stable) Full chip erase: ON (clears old junk config) Manual baud: off (auto is fine) [ Load Firmware Online ] -> [ Flash Firmware ] Programming: 100% — Verifying... OK

Use Full chip erase when in doubt; you'll reconfigure from scratch but avoid leftover settings causing weird behavior. After flashing, the board reboots and reconnects.

Configurator tab tour

  • Setup — the 3D model that mirrors your quad; calibrate accelerometer, reset, see arming flags.
  • Ports — assign UART functions (serial RX, GPS, VTX).
  • Configuration / Motors / Modes / Receiver — core flight setup.
  • OSD — on-screen display layout.
  • PID Tuning — rates, PIDs, filters.
  • CLI — the text command line for advanced edits; diff all dumps your full config, save writes and reboots.

On the Setup tab, tilt the physical quad and watch the model. If it moves the wrong way, your board orientation (Yaw 180 etc.) needs setting in Configuration. A responsive, correctly-oriented model is your green light to proceed.

Back up first.
Before any flash or big change, open CLI and run diff all, then copy the output to a text file. That's your restore point.
▸Hands-On

Flash Betaflight and verify a live, correctly-oriented model.

  1. Install Configurator + drivers; connect FC via USB (props OFF).
  2. Look up your exact FC target name in its docs.
  3. Enter DFU, select target + latest stable, enable Full chip erase, flash.
  4. Reconnect, open Setup, tilt the quad, confirm the model matches. Screenshot it.

title: Ports & UARTs: Wiring Peripherals in Software
html:
What a UART is

A UART (Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter) is a hardware serial port on the FC, labeled TX1/RX1, TX2/RX2, etc. Each peripheral that talks serially — your radio receiver, a VTX with control, a GPS — needs its own UART. The Ports tab is where you tell the firmware what is plugged into which UART. Physical wiring alone does nothing; the software must enable the matching function.

The TX/RX cross rule

Serial is wired crossed: the peripheral's TX goes to the FC's RX and vice versa. If your receiver isn't detected, a swapped TX/RX is the most common cause. Note which UART number a pad belongs to (the silkscreen says R2 = RX of UART2).

Common assignments

PeripheralPorts tab columnNotes
Receiver (ELRS/Crossfire/etc.)Serial RX (the toggle)Protocol set in Configuration tab
VTX control (Tramp/SmartAudio)Peripherals → VTX (Tramp) or VTX (TBS SmartAudio)Single wire to a TX pad
GPSSensor Input → GPSSet baud (often 115200) and enable GPS in Configuration
ESC telemetrySensor Input → ESCFor RPM/temp from BLHeli_32/AM32
Ports tab
UART1 Configuration/MSP 115200 SerialRX off Periph off UART2 Config/MSP off SerialRX ON Periph off # receiver UART4 Config/MSP off SerialRX off Periph VTX SmartAudio UART6 Config/MSP off SensorIn GPS 115200 # gps [ Save and Reboot ]

Important gotchas

  • Leave UART1 (or whichever has the USB MSP) alone unless you know it's free — it's often your Configuration/MSP link.
  • After enabling Serial RX here, go to Configuration and pick the receiver protocol (e.g., CRSF for ELRS/Crossfire). The Ports tab only opens the lane; Configuration names the traffic.
  • SmartAudio/Tramp is a single wire to a TX pad; you still assign it on a full UART column.
  • One function per UART. You can't run a receiver and VTX control on the same port.
Verify, don't assume.
After Save and Reboot, check the Receiver tab for moving bars, the GPS tab for a sat count, and your VTX menu for control. If a peripheral is dead, suspect TX/RX swap or wrong UART first.
▸Hands-On

Map your physical wiring into the Ports tab.

  1. Trace each peripheral wire to its UART number on the FC silkscreen.
  2. Enable Serial RX for the receiver's UART; set protocol in Configuration.
  3. Assign VTX control and GPS to their UARTs; set GPS baud.
  4. Save and Reboot, then confirm receiver bars, sat count, and VTX control all respond.

title: Receiver Setup, Modes & Arming
html:
Verify your channels first

Open the Receiver tab. Move each stick and watch the bars. The convention is AETR: Roll (A), Pitch (E), Throttle (T), Yaw (R), then Aux channels. Confirm:

  • Each stick moves the correct bar in the correct direction.
  • Centered sticks read about 1500; endpoints reach roughly 1000 and 2000.
  • Throttle low = ~1000, full = ~2000. If reversed, fix the channel map (or radio), not by guessing.

Set the Channel Map dropdown to match your radio's output order. ELRS/Crossfire on CRSF typically reports clean values automatically.

Props OFF for all of this.
You are about to make the quad armable. Remove every propeller before assigning Arm and testing modes. Treat an armed quad as a spinning hazard even on the bench.

Assigning modes

Go to the Modes tab. Modes are activated by Aux channel ranges (a switch position on your radio). The essentials:

ModePurpose
ARMEnables motors. Map to a momentary or 2-position switch.
ANGLESelf-leveling (beginner). Releasing sticks levels the quad.
HORIZONSelf-levels but allows full flips.
ACRO (no mode)Rate mode — no self-level. The default when ANGLE/HORIZON are off.
BEEPERFind-my-quad buzzer.
FLIP OVER AFTER CRASH (Turtle)Reverses motors to right an upside-down quad.

Setting the switch ranges

For each mode, click Add Range, pick the Aux channel, then flip the physical switch and watch the yellow marker. Drag the range so it covers only the switch position you want. A good ARM range is ~1750–2100 on a 2-position switch, leaving a clear OFF zone.

Modes tab
ARM AUX1 range 1750 - 2100 # switch UP = armed ANGLE AUX2 range 1300 - 1700 # mid = self-level ACRO (no switch — active when ANGLE off) BEEPER AUX3 range 1750 - 2100 Arming flags: throttle high, RX loss (clear these before arming)

Arming safety checks

  • Betaflight refuses to arm if throttle isn't low, if the quad isn't level (when configured), or if there are arming flags (shown on Setup tab and in the OSD).
  • Set up failsafe (Configuration / Failsafe tab) to Drop so motors cut on signal loss — never let a lost quad keep flying toward people.
  • Test arming with the radio only, props off: flip ARM, confirm the OSD/Setup shows ARMED, then disarm. The motors should idle, not jump.
Disarm habit.
Make ARM a flip-up switch you can reach instantly, and build the muscle memory to flip it OFF the moment something feels wrong.
▸Hands-On

Set channels and assign arming + flight modes, props OFF.

  1. In Receiver, verify AETR direction, center 1500, throttle low/high.
  2. In Modes, assign ARM to a switch with a clean 1750–2100 range.
  3. Add ANGLE on a separate switch; leave the OFF position as Acro.
  4. Confirm failsafe = Drop, then arm/disarm via radio and watch the state change.

title: Configuring the OSD: Voltage, Timer & Warnings
html:
What the OSD is

The OSD (On-Screen Display) overlays flight data onto your video feed so you see it in the goggles. Two flavors exist: classic analog/MAX7456 character OSD, and digital (MSP) OSD used by DJI/HDZero/Walksnail, which renders the same elements through the air unit. Setup is similar in the Configurator's OSD tab; digital systems give you more resolution and font choices.

The must-have elements

You can drag dozens of elements onto the layout, but clutter kills awareness. The non-negotiables:

ElementWhy it matters
Battery voltage (avg cell or pack)Your fuel gauge — land before sag drops cells under load.
Flight timer (on-time / arm-time)Budget flight to battery, not luck. Use the armed timer.
RSSI / Link Quality (LQ)On ELRS, watch LQ — falling LQ warns of failsafe before video breaks up.
mAh drawn (with a current sensor)More accurate than voltage under throttle; great for sizing flights.
Warnings lineShows arming flags, low battery, RX loss in plain text.

Reading sag, not just resting voltage

A 6S pack reads 25.2V full (4.20V/cell) and is empty around 3.5V/cell resting. Under throttle the voltage sags, then recovers when you ease off. Judge by the lowest you see under load and the resting value after landing — aim to land with cells around 3.7–3.8V resting. Set the OSD to show average cell voltage so the number is cell-count independent.

Warnings & thresholds

In the OSD tab's lower panel set:

OSD warnings
Warn cell voltage: 3.50 V # OSD flashes / changes color Min cell voltage: 3.30 V Max cell voltage: 4.20 V Timer alarm: 4:00 # nudge to land RSSI warning: enabled Arming-flag display: enabled

When voltage hits the warning, the value blinks — that's your signal to head home. Position warnings centrally so they catch your eye; put always-on data (voltage, timer, LQ) along the bottom corners where they don't block the framing.

Calibrate voltage.
Compare the OSD voltage to a meter on the battery. If it's off, set vbat_scale in CLI (or the Power tab) so the reading is truthful — a lying fuel gauge causes crashed packs.
Don't over-discharge.
Pulling a LiPo below ~3.3V/cell under load damages it and can lead to puffing. A trustworthy OSD voltage + timer is how you avoid it. Retire any puffed pack.
▸Hands-On

Lay out a clean, safety-first OSD and screenshot it.

  1. Add average-cell voltage, armed timer, and RSSI/LQ; place them in corners.
  2. Add a warnings element centered for arming-flag and low-batt alerts.
  3. Set warn cell = 3.50V and timer alarm = your expected flight time.
  4. Verify OSD voltage against a meter; adjust vbat scale if needed. Screenshot the layout.

title: Rates: Dialing In How the Quad Responds
html:
Rates ≠ PIDs

A common confusion: rates control how fast the quad rotates for a given stick input; PIDs control how well it follows that command. Rates are pure feel and personal preference — there is no "correct" rate, only what suits your style and skill. They live in the PID Tuning → Rates sub-tab.

The three knobs

ParameterWhat it does
RC RateOverall sensitivity; scales the whole curve. Higher = faster everywhere.
Super RateAdds rotation speed at the stick ends, keeping center calm. Sets the max spin rate.
RC ExpoSoftens the center for fine control without lowering the max.

The headline number is max rotation rate in degrees/second, shown live on the rate curve as you drag sliders. A gentle beginner setup might top out around 400–500°/s; aggressive freestyle commonly runs 800–1000+°/s; racers tune yaw lower for clean cornering.

Rate types

Betaflight offers several rate models: Actual, Betaflight, QuickRates, etc. Actual Rates is the most intuitive for learning because you directly set Center Sensitivity and Max Rate in real units — what you ask for is what you get.

PID Tuning — Rates (Actual)
Roll Pitch Yaw Center: 120 120 100 # deg/s near center — gentle Max Rate: 500 500 400 # deg/s at full stick Expo: 0.40 0.40 0.40 # calmer center Beginner profile: smooth, forgiving, predictable.

A beginner-friendly profile

  • Keep max rate ~450–550°/s on roll/pitch — fast enough to maneuver, slow enough to not over-rotate.
  • Add expo ~0.3–0.4 so small stick movements are smooth for line-holding and cruising.
  • Set yaw a bit lower than roll/pitch for stable turns.
  • Fly it in the simulator or in Angle mode first; only push rates up once your hands are steady.

Tuning toward agility

Want it snappier? Raise Max Rate (more spin at full deflection) and/or Center Sensitivity (quicker initial response). Want flips to whip? Push max rate toward 900–1000°/s. If the quad feels twitchy at center, add expo rather than dropping max rate — you keep the top end while calming small inputs.

Change one thing.
Adjust a single axis or knob per session and fly the same line. You can't feel what you can't isolate.
Sim before sky.
Test new rates in a simulator (Liftoff, Velocidrone, DRL) or in Angle mode in open space. A rate that's too hot in a tight spot causes crashes into people or property.
▸Hands-On

Build a beginner rate profile and document the curve.

  1. Switch to Actual Rates; set max ~500 roll/pitch, ~400 yaw.
  2. Add expo ~0.35; read the max°/s off the live curve and write it down.
  3. Fly it (sim or Angle mode) and note the feel.
  4. Describe exactly what you'd change (which knob, which axis) to get more agility.

title: PID Tuning Basics & Filters
html:
What a PID controller does

Every loop, the FC compares what you asked for (your stick = target rotation rate) to what the gyro measured (actual rotation). The difference is the error. The PID controller turns that error into motor corrections using three terms working together.

TermJobToo highToo low
P (Proportional)Reacts to current error — the main corrective force.Fast oscillation, hot motorsSloppy, sluggish, drifts off line
I (Integral)Holds the target over time; fights wind/drift and prop wash.Slow wobble, bounce-back, drifty feelWon't hold attitude; pushed off in wind
D (Derivative)Dampens — predicts and brakes overshoot.Hot motors, high-freq buzz, noise sensitivityBounce-back / overshoot after flicks

Symptoms and what they mean

  • Fast, high-pitched oscillation + hot motors → P (or D) too high, or noise getting into D. Lower P/D or improve filtering.
  • Bounce-back after a flick or punch-out → not enough D damping (or P too high). Raise D a little.
  • Slow wallowing wobble, mushy feel → I too high, or P too low. Reassess the balance.
  • Drifts off heading / blown around in wind → I too low.
  • Hot motors with no obvious shake → almost always noise reaching the motors through D. This is a filter problem, not a PID problem.

Why filters exist

The gyro picks up real rotation and vibration noise from motors, props, and frame resonance. The D term amplifies high-frequency noise — feed it dirty data and it commands rapid motor changes that heat the motors and can cause runaway oscillation. Filters (mostly low-pass on gyro and D-term, plus RPM filtering driven by ESC telemetry) strip that noise before it reaches the controller.

Filters (concept)
Gyro raw -> RPM filter -> Gyro LPF -> PID -> D-term LPF -> Motors Less filtering = lower latency but more noise risk More filtering = smoother but adds delay (mushy feel) Filtering is a tradeoff: clean signal vs. propagation delay.

Modern Betaflight makes this easier

Recent versions ship with good defaults and a slider-based tune: a master multiplier plus damping/feel sliders, and RPM filtering (requires bidirectional DShot + ESC telemetry) that targets motor-frequency noise precisely. For most builds, leave filters near default, enable RPM filtering, and nudge the PID sliders rather than editing raw numbers.

Heat = warning.
After a flight, if a motor is too hot to hold comfortably, land and stop. Hot motors usually mean noise in D or too-high P/D — flying on burns motors and can cause mid-air failure.
Tune order.
Fix mechanical issues first (balanced props, tight screws, no soft mounts loose), enable RPM filtering, then adjust PIDs. A clean build needs little tuning.
▸Hands-On

Write a 3-symptom tune troubleshooting guide.

  1. Symptom 1 — hot motors: state likely cause (noise in D / high P-D) and first fix (enable RPM filter, lower D).
  2. Symptom 2 — fast oscillation: cause (P or D too high) and first fix.
  3. Symptom 3 — drift / won't hold in wind: cause (I too low) and first fix.
  4. Note which to check mechanically before touching numbers.

title: ESC Firmware (BLHeli_S/32) & Calibration
html:
The ESC runs its own firmware

Each ESC (or each channel of a 4-in-1) runs firmware that turns the FC's motor command into the three-phase switching that drives the motor. The main families:

FirmwareHardwareNotes
BLHeli_SOlder 8-bit ESCsConfigured with BLHeliSuite; Bluejay custom firmware adds bidirectional DShot (RPM filtering) and higher PWM.
BLHeli_3232-bit ESCs (now closed/legacy)Rich features, telemetry, current limiting; configured via BLHeli_32 Suite.
AM32Modern open-source 32-bitOpen replacement for BLHeli_32; configured via the AM32 configurator.

Why update / flash ESC firmware

  • RPM filtering needs bidirectional DShot — BLHeli_S boards need Bluejay; 32-bit needs a recent BLHeli_32/AM32 build.
  • Bug fixes for desyncs (a desync = motor stutter/stall mid-flight).
  • Set protocol (use DShot300/600, not analog PWM), motor timing, and demag compensation.
PROPS OFF — no exceptions.
Everything in this lesson spins motors. Remove all four props and keep hands and face clear before connecting to any ESC tool or pressing a motor slider. Secure the quad so it can't move.

Checking firmware & motor direction

Connect the FC over USB and open the ESC configurator (BLHeli/Bluejay/AM32). It reads each ESC and shows the firmware version — confirm all four match. To set rotation direction you have two routes:

  • In the ESC tool: set "Motor Direction" to Normal/Reversed per ESC.
  • In Betaflight Motors tab (easier): enable bidirectional DShot, then use the per-motor direction toggle and the spin test.

Quads use a fixed spin pattern ("props in" or "props out"). In the Motors tab, click the motor map, spin each motor at low throttle, and confirm it spins the correct way and that the labeled motor is the physical one you expect.

Motors tab — direction check (PROPS OFF)
[x] I understand props are removed Protocol: DShot600 Bidirectional DShot: ON M1 -> CW M2 -> CCW M3 -> CCW M4 -> CW Spin each at idle, confirm direction matches your prop config.

Do you still "calibrate" ESCs?

Classic ESC throttle calibration (teaching the ESC min/max throttle endpoints) applies to analog PWM ESCs. With DShot — the modern standard — throttle is digital and no calibration is needed. So on any current build, skip ESC throttle calibration; just confirm DShot is selected.

Accelerometer calibration

The accelerometer tells the FC which way is level — needed for Angle/Horizon modes and a level horizon in the OSD. To calibrate: place the quad on a truly flat, level surface, open the Setup tab, and click Calibrate Accelerometer. Hold it dead still for the count. A bad calibration shows as a tilted horizon or drift in self-level modes.

Level matters.
Use a real level surface (check with a bubble level). If the bench is tilted, your "level" will be tilted too — and Angle mode will pull to one side.
▸Hands-On

Verify ESC firmware + directions, then calibrate the accelerometer. PROPS OFF.

  1. Open Bluejay/BLHeli/AM32; confirm all four ESCs share the same firmware version.
  2. Confirm DShot600 + bidirectional DShot in the Motors tab.
  3. Spin each motor at idle; correct any wrong directions; log the before/after.
  4. Set the quad on a level surface and run Calibrate Accelerometer; verify a flat horizon after.

title: Reading Blackbox Logs & an Intro to INAV/GPS Builds
html:
What Blackbox is

Blackbox records high-rate flight data — gyro, setpoint (your command), PID terms, motor outputs, RC input, voltage — so you can diagnose tune and mechanical problems instead of guessing. It logs to onboard flash (a chip on the FC, limited size) or an SD card (much larger). Enable it in the Blackbox tab, pick the device, set a sane logging rate (e.g., 2kHz), then fly and download the .bbl/.bfl file.

Opening a log

Open the file in the Blackbox Explorer. You get scrolling traces over time. The key traces and what to look for:

TraceRead it for
Gyro (filtered) vs. SetpointHow well actual rotation tracks your command. Big gaps = poor tune.
Gyro raw / unfilteredVibration and noise floor — fuzzy thick lines = mechanical noise.
D-termSpiky D = noise being amplified (the hot-motor culprit).
Motor outputsOne motor pinned high = imbalance, bent prop, or mount issue.
RC Command / RSSI / vbatDropouts, sag, or input glitches.

Spotting noise vs. oscillation

Reading traces
HEALTHY: gyro ~~~ follows setpoint, thin clean lines NOISE: gyro line is fuzzy/thick even when not commanded OSCILLATE: regular sine-like wobble after a stick stop MECH: one motor output much higher than the others
  • Noise looks like fuzz/thickness on the gyro and D traces with no commanded motion — points to vibration, bad prop, or under-filtering.
  • Oscillation is a periodic wobble (often after a flick) — points to PID balance (too much P/D, or bounce-back from too little D).
  • The Spectral Analyzer (frequency view) pinpoints a noise peak: a motor-RPM peak says enable/check RPM filtering; a sharp fixed peak can be frame resonance.
Log smart.
Fly a deliberate test: hover, a few punches, some flips, a hard stop. You need command variety to see how the quad responds.

When to move to INAV

Betaflight is built for hands-on flying. The moment you want the aircraft to know where it is and act on it, look at INAV:

  • GPS rescue / return-to-home that actually navigates home (Betaflight has basic GPS Rescue, INAV is more capable for cruising).
  • Position hold & altitude hold for stable long-range or cinematic loitering.
  • Waypoint missions — fly a programmed path.
  • Fixed-wing planes — INAV handles airplanes, flying wings, and their navigation modes far better than Betaflight.

INAV needs a GPS + compass (magnetometer) module and a clean compass mount away from current-carrying wires. The Configurator is similar to Betaflight's, with extra Navigation and Mission tabs. Tune feel is calmer by design — appropriate for GPS cruisers and wings, not race-quad sharpness.

Autonomy ≠ exemption.
GPS missions and RTH must still obey altitude limits, line-of-sight/BVLOS rules, Remote ID, and no-fly zones. Verify current FAA or your national CAA rules before any automated or long-range flight.
▸Hands-On

Record/open a Blackbox log and interpret one trace.

  1. Enable Blackbox (flash or SD), set ~2kHz, fly a varied test pattern (props on, safe area) — or open a sample log.
  2. Download the file and open it in Blackbox Explorer.
  3. Find one trace showing noise or oscillation (gyro fuzz, spiky D, or a pinned motor).
  4. Write 2-3 sentences interpreting it and the first fix you'd try.
